text: - muscular injections.7 Octreotide may be more effective than lanreotide, but not all formulations have been com- pared.8 Octreotide can also be given by subcutaneous in- jection, but must be given three times daily, making it less attractive for long-term therapy. There have been some promising reports of the use of somatostatin analogues for primary therapy, but when there is visual or neurological compromise then surgery is preferred because drug thera- py may not provide enough tumour shrinkage to relieve pressure on the optic chiasm.7,9 There is some data to sug- gest that pre-operative use of somatostatin analogues could improve cardiovascular, respiratory, and metabolic functions and hence reduce morbidity associated with sur- gery, and improve remission rates, but further study is needed.7,8,10 Dopaminergics can produce a paradoxical re- duction in growth hormone secretion in some patients with acromegaly, providing symptomatic relief. Bromocriptine produces acceptable suppression of growth hormone se- cretion in less than 20% of patients.9 A small study of quinagolide reported the normalisation of hormonal values in about 44% of patients, which was better than the poor responses to a depot preparation of bromocriptine, or ca- bergoline.11 A later, open study, however, found that caber- goline produced a good response in about 40% of pa- tients.12 Dopaminergics are generally added to somatostatin analogue therapy5 and may be most useful in patients with associated hyperprolactinaemia.2,5,8 Pegviso- mant is a growth hormone-receptor antagonist that may be used when other therapies have failed or are inappropri- ate.2,8,13 It is reported14,15 to lower IGF-I concentrations, improve signs and symptoms of acromegaly, and be well tolerated. Pegvisomant does not reduce growth hormone concentrations so these patients must be monitored by IGF-I measurement.4 The addition of pegvisomant has also been reported to normalise IGF-I concentrations in patients with persistently elevated levels during somato- statin analogue therapy.16 Tumour regression induced by radiotherapy is a possible alternative when surgery cannot be performed, there is re- sidual pituitary disease after surgery, or medical therapy has failed.2,5,6 Although it reduces growth hormone con- centrations in about 90% of patients3 and tumour recur- rence is rare5 its effects are slow and it often produces hy- popituitarism. Some consider these to be disadvantages and prefer to use drug treatment for management of tu- mours that persist after surgery.5 Since it may take several years for growth hormone concentrations to fall, drug ther- apy is also given until the effects of radiation therapy are satisfactory.2,5 1.
